_: Besselian elements for solar eclipses, transcribed from NASA's SEdata pages (public domain, eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEsearch/SEdata.php?Ecl=YYYYMMDD). Conventions: t is hours from t0_tdt_hours; mu in degrees; x/y/d in degrees for d, dimensionless for x/y/l1/l2; longitude EAST POSITIVE.

eclipses._note: The deepest-past anchor, and the corpus's oldest recorded eclipse (the default year filter in js/permalink.js starts at -762). NASA titles it '-762 June 15' in the JULIAN calendar; date_utc is the proleptic Gregorian equivalent -000762-06-07 (JD 1442903), matching events/-000762-06-07.json. Added specifically to test whether the AE-vs-NASA lunar offset scales as T^2 — one ancient sample cannot distinguish a T^2 law from a constant. Same d3 PHP warning as the 1082 entry; d3=0 assumed. Note delta_T here is 21210.6 s (5h53m), so any confusion of the UT and TDT frames shows up as a ~5.9 h error rather than a subtle one — a useful frame tripwire.
eclipses._verified: Transcribed by direct browser read of the rendered SEdata page. Self-consistency: solving x*x' + y*y' = 0 on these polynomials must reproduce NASA's stated 14:07:32 TDT / 8:14:01 UT and gamma 0.2715 — asserted by tools/test-cross-validate.mjs as the Path-A transcription self-check.

eclipses._note: The only pre-modern entry here, added as ground truth for ancient-eclipse cross-validation. NASA's page (Ecl=10820430) titles this '1082 April 30' in the JULIAN calendar; date_utc is the proleptic Gregorian equivalent 1082-05-06 (+6 d in the 11th century), matching the events/ and solar.json keys. NASA prints 135.6 W; sign flipped to -135.6 per the EAST POSITIVE convention declared above. NASA's d-column cubic cell emits a PHP warning (undefined $_5MCSE_besselian_d3) and renders as 0.0000000 — d3=0 matches every other entry here and is assumed correct. Note 5MCSE derives its ancient dT from Morrison & Stephenson (2004), NOT from the Espenak-Meeus 2006 polynomials that astronomy-engine implements: the two differ by ~10 s at 1082 (~0.04 deg of longitude), which is far too small to explain the ~1.13 deg greatest-eclipse offset this entry was added to diagnose.
eclipses._verified: Transcribed by direct browser read of the rendered SEdata page (not a WebFetch summary), cross-checked value-by-value. Self-consistency confirmed by hand: solving x*x' + y*y' = 0 on these polynomials gives t = +0.1042 h -> greatest eclipse 20:06:15 TDT and gamma = 0.7301, both reproducing NASA's stated values exactly.

_validation_note: Values transcribed from NASA SEpath2001 central-line column for 2017-08-21. Times that the WebFetch returned for non-30-min boundaries turned out to be from the *northern-limit* column (~0.5° lat above central line, matching half the path width); those rows are excluded. The kept rows are spot-verified against NASA's 2-min table.
